questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of metal, of 25g mass moves down without acceleration when the plane is inclined at an angle of $30^{}^{\circ}$. When the inclination is increased by $30^{}^{\circ}$, find the downward acceleration of the block.
questions.solution:
When the block moves down without acceleration at an angle $\theta = 30^{}^{\circ}$, the net force is zero.

$mg \sin 30^{}^{\circ} = \mu_k mg \cos 30^{}^{\circ}$

$\mu_k = \tan 30^{}^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

When the inclination is increased by $30^{}^{\circ}$, the new angle is $\theta' = 60^{}^{\circ}$.

The downward acceleration $a$ is given by:

$ma = mg \sin 60^{}^{\circ} - \mu_k mg \cos 60^{}^{\circ}$

$a = g \left( \sin60^{}^{\circ} - \mu_k \cos 60^{}^{\circ} \right)$

Substituting the values of $\mu_k$ and $g = 9.8\ ms^{-2}$:

$a = 9.8 \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \right)$

$a = 9.8 \left( \dfrac{3 - 1}{2\sqrt{3}} \right) = \dfrac{9.8}{\sqrt{3}}$

$a = \dfrac{9.8}{1.732} \approx5.66\ ms^{-2}$

Answer: $5.66\ ms^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the maximum speed with which a vehicle can take the turn on a curved frictionless smooth road of width 4 m , without skidding, if the radius of the circular curve of the road is 9 m and the outer edge of the road above the inner edge is 40 cm high? [given $g=\mathrm{1 0} \mathrm{ms}^{-2}$ ]
questions.solution:
For a vehicle moving on a banked road without skidding, the required centripetal force is provided by the horizontal component of the normal reaction. The angle of banking $\theta$ is given by $\tan \theta = \dfrac{h}{b}$, where $h$ is the height of the outer edge above the inner edge and $b$ is the width of the road.

Given $h = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.4 \text{ m}$ and $b = 4 \text{ m}$, we have $\tan \theta = \dfrac{0.4}{4} = 0.1$.

The maximum speed $v$ for a banked road without friction is given by $v = \sqrt{rg \tan \theta}$, where $r$ is the radius of the curve and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Substituting the given values $r = 9 \text{ m}$, $g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}$, and $\tan \theta = 0.1$:

$v = \sqrt{9 \times 10 \times 0.1} = \sqrt{9} = 3 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{3} \mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Pick out the weakest force from the four given fundamental forces in nature.
questions.solution:
The four fundamental forces in nature are the strong nuclear force, the electromagnetic force, the weak nuclear force, and the gravitational force.

The relative strengths of these forces are typically compared by considering the interaction between two protons at a distance of $10^{-15}$ m. The strong nuclear force is the strongest, followed by the electromagnetic force, then the weak nuclear force, and finally the gravitational force.

The gravitational force is the weakest among the four fundamental forces, as its coupling constant is extremely small compared to the others.

Answer: Gravitational force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass 125 kg just slides down a rough inclined plane that rises 1 m in every 2 m. What is the angle of friction?
questions.solution:
The plane rises 1 m in every 2 m, so:

$\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = 30°$

When a body just slides down, it is at limiting equilibrium, so angle of friction $\phi =$ angle of inclination $\theta$.

$\phi = 30° = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ radians

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coin is placed on a disc rotating with an angular velocity $\omega$. The co-efficient of friction between the disc and the coin is $\mu$. The maximum distance of the coin from the centre of the disc up to which it will rotate with the disc is
questions.solution:
For the coin to rotate with the disc without slipping, the centripetal force required for circular motion must be provided by the static frictional force.

Let $m$ be the mass of the coin, $r$ be the distance from the centre, and $\omega$ be the angular velocity. The centripetal force is $F_c = m \omega^2 r$.

The maximum static frictional force available is $f_\max = \mu N$, where $N = mg$ is the normal force. Thus, $f_\max = \mu mg$.

For the coin to remain stationary relative to the disc, the condition is $F_c \le f_\max$.

$m \omega^2 r \le \mu mg$.

Solving for the maximum distance $r$, we get $r \le \dfrac{\mu g}{\omega^2}$.

Therefore, the maximum distance is $r_\max = \dfrac{\mu g}{\omega^2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu g}{\omega^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass 10 kg is moving up on an inclined plane of $30^{{}^{\circ}}$ with an acceleration $2 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$. Find the force required, if the coefficient of friction between the object and the plane surface is $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$, [given $g=10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ ].
questions.solution:
The forces acting on the body of mass $m = 10$ kg moving up the inclined plane are the applied force $F$ (acting up the plane), the component of gravitational force $mg \sin \theta$ (acting down the plane), and the frictional force $f_k$ (acting down the plane).

The equation of motion is $F - mg \sin \theta - f_k = ma$.

The normal force $N$ exerted by the plane is $N = mg \cos \theta$.

The frictional force is $f_k = \mu N = \mu mg \cos \theta$.

Given $m = 10$ kg, $g = 10$ ms^{-2}$, $\theta = 30^{{}^{\circ}}$, $a = 2$ ms^{-2}$, and $\mu = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$.

Calculating the components:
$mg \sin 30^{{}^{\circ}} = 10 \times 10 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 50$ N.
$f_k = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6} \times 10 \times 10 \times \cos 30^{{}^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6} \times 100 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{3 \times 100}{12} = \dfrac{300}{12} = 25$ N.

Substituting these values into the equation of motion:
$F - 50 - 25 = 10 \times 2$
$F - 75 = 20$
$F = 95$ N.

Answer: 95 N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cube bar slides thrice the time with friction than that without friction when it slides on an inclined plane of inclination $45^{{}^{\circ}}$. The coefficient of friction between the block and the surface is
questions.solution:
For a block sliding down an inclined plane of angle $\theta$ without friction, the acceleration is $a_1 = g \sin \theta$. The time taken to cover a distance $s$ is $t_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{a_1}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{g \sin \theta}}$.

For a block sliding down with friction, the acceleration is $a_2 = g(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)$. The time taken to cover the same distance $s$ is $t_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{a_2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{g(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)}}$.

Given $t_2 = 3t_1$, we have $\sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{g(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)}} = 3 \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{g \sin \theta}}$.

Squaring both sides, $\dfrac{1}{\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta} = \dfrac{9}{\sin \theta}$.

Rearranging gives $9(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta) = \sin \theta$, which simplifies to $8 \sin \theta = 9 \mu \cos \theta$.

Thus, $\mu = \dfrac{8}{9} \tan \theta$.

Given $\theta = 45^{{}^{\circ}}$, $\tan 45^{{}^{\circ}} = 1$, so $\mu = \dfrac{8}{9} \approx 0.888$.

Answer: 0.88

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body initially at rest undergoes rectilinear motion. The forcetime (F-t) graph for the motion of the body is given below. Find the linear momentum gained by the body in $2 \mathrm{ s}$.
questions.solution:
The impulse $J$ delivered to a body is equal to the change in its linear momentum $\Delta p$.

The impulse is given by the area under the force-time ($F-t$) graph.

For the interval $t = 0$ to $t = 2$ s, the graph represents a semi-circle below the time axis with radius $r = 1$ s and amplitude $A = 4$ N.

The area of this semi-circle is $A_{area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \pi r^2$.

Since the area is below the time axis, the impulse is negative: $J = -\dfrac{1}{2} \pi (1)^2 = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ N-s.

The magnitude of the linear momentum gained is $|J| = \left| -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right| = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ N-s.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \mathrm{ N}-\mathrm{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Action and reaction can never balance out because
options: They are equal in magnitude but not opposite always.
They are unequal in magnitudes even though opposite in direction
Though they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction they act on different bodies.
questions.solution:
According to Newton's third law of motion, for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

These two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

However, the fundamental reason they do not balance each other out is that they act on two different bodies. Since the forces are applied to different objects, they cannot result in the net force on a single body being zero.

Answer: Though they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction they act on different bodies.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A stone of mass $2 \mathrm{ kg}$ is hung from the ceiling of the room using two strings. If the strings make an angle $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ and $30^{{}^{\circ}}$ respectively with the horizontal surface of the roof then the tension on the longer string is : $g=10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$
questions.solution:
The string making $30°$ with the horizontal is longer. Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be tensions in strings at $60°$ and $30°$ respectively. Weight $W = mg = 20$ N.

Horizontal equilibrium:
$T_1\cos60° = T_2\cos30°$
$T_1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = T_2 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow T_1 = \sqrt{3}T_2$

Vertical equilibrium:
$T_1\sin60° + T_2\sin30° = 20$

Substituting $T_1 = \sqrt{3}T_2$:
$\sqrt{3}T_2 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + T_2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 20$

$T_2\left(\dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 20 \Rightarrow 2T_2 = 20 \Rightarrow T_2 = 10$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}}, \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}}$ and $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{C}}$ are three forces acting at point $\mathrm{P}$ as shown in figure. The whole system is in equilibrium state. The magnitude of $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}}$ is
questions.solution:
The system is in equilibrium at point P. We resolve the forces $F_A$ and $F_B$ into their horizontal and vertical components.

For horizontal equilibrium:
$F_B \cos(45^{{}^{\circ}}) - F_A \cos(30^{{}^{\circ}}) = 0$
$F_B \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = F_A \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
$F_B = F_A \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}} = F_A \sqrt{1.5}$

For vertical equilibrium:
$F_A \sin(30^{{}^{\circ}}) + F_B \sin(45^{{}^{\circ}}) = F_C$
Since $F_C = 100$ N, we have:
$F_A \sin(30^{{}^{\circ}}) + (F_A \sqrt{1.5}) \sin(45^{{}^{\circ}}) = 100$
$F_A (0.5) + F_A \sqrt{1.5} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 100$
$F_A (0.5) + F_A \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 100$
$F_A (0.5) + F_A \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 100$
$F_A (0.5 + 0.866) = 100$
$F_A (1.366) = 100$
$F_A = \dfrac{100}{1.366} \approx 73.206$ N.

Answer: 73.2 N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the resultant of all external forces acting on a system of particles is zero, then from an inertial frame one can surely say that
options: Potential energy of the system does not change in time.
Kinetic energy of the system does not change in time.
Angular momentum of the system does not change in time
Linear momentum of the system does not change in time
questions.solution:
The net external force acting on a system of particles is given by the rate of change of the total linear momentum of the system, expressed as $\vec{F}_{ext} = \dfrac{d\vec{P}}{dt}$.

Given that the resultant of all external forces is zero, $\vec{F}_{ext} = 0$.

Substituting this into the equation, we get $\dfrac{d\vec{P}}{dt} = 0$.

Integrating with respect to time, we find that the total linear momentum $\vec{P}$ of the system remains constant over time. This is the principle of conservation of linear momentum.

Answer: Linear momentum of the system does not change in time

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A spring of force constant $k$ is cut into lengths of ratio $1 : 3 : 4$. They are connected in series and the new force constant is $k'$. Then they are connected in parallel and force constant is $k''$. Then $k' : k''$ is
questions.solution:
Let the total length of the spring be $L$. The spring is cut into three parts with lengths $l_1 = \dfrac{1}{8}L$, $l_2 = \dfrac{3}{8}L$, and $l_3 = \dfrac{4}{8}L$.

The force constant of a spring is inversely proportional to its length, $k \propto \dfrac{1}{l}$. Thus, $k_1 = 8k$, $k_2 = \dfrac{8}{3}k$, and $k_3 = 2k$.

When connected in series, the equivalent force constant $k'$ is given by $\dfrac{1}{k'} = \dfrac{1}{k_1} + \dfrac{1}{k_2} + \dfrac{1}{k_3} = \dfrac{1}{8k} + \dfrac{3}{8k} + \dfrac{1}{2k} = \dfrac{1+3+4}{8k} = \dfrac{8}{8k} = \dfrac{1}{k}$. Therefore, $k' = k$.

When connected in parallel, the equivalent force constant $k''$ is given by $k'' = k_1 + k_2 + k_3 = 8k + \dfrac{8}{3}k + 2k = 10k + \dfrac{8}{3}k = \dfrac{30k + 8k}{3} = \dfrac{38k}{3}$.

The ratio $k' : k'' = k : \dfrac{38k}{3} = 1 : \dfrac{38}{3} = 3 : 38$.

The ratio is $3:38$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A balloon with mass $m$ is descending down with an acceleration $a$ (where, $a < g$ ). How much mass should be removed from it so that it starts moving up with an acceleration $a$ ?
questions.solution:
Let $F$ be the upward buoyant force acting on the balloon. When the balloon of mass $m$ is descending with acceleration $a$, the equation of motion is $mg - F = ma$.

From this, $F = m(g - a)$.

Let $m'$ be the mass to be removed, so the new mass is $m - m'$. When the balloon moves up with acceleration $a$, the equation of motion is $F - (m - m')g = (m - m')a$.

Substituting $F = m(g - a)$ into the equation, we get $m(g - a) - (m - m')g = (m - m')a$.

$mg - ma - mg + m'g = ma - m'a$.

$m'g + m'a = 2ma$.

$m'(g + a) = 2ma$.

$m' = \dfrac{2ma}{g + a}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2 m a}{g+a}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $With what minimum acceleration can a fireman slide down a rope while breaking strength of the rope is \dfrac{2}{3}$ of the weight?
questions.solution:
Let $m$ be the mass of the fireman and $g$ be the acceleration due to gravity. The weight of the fireman is $W = mg$.

The breaking strength of the rope is given as $T_\max = \dfrac{2}{3} mg$.

When the fireman slides down with an acceleration $a$, the equation of motion is $mg - T = ma$, where $T$ is the tension in the rope.

To prevent the rope from breaking, the tension $T$ must not exceed $T_\max$. Thus, $T \le \dfrac{2}{3} mg$.

Substituting the maximum tension into the equation of motion: $mg - \dfrac{2}{3} mg = ma$.

Solving for $a$: $\dfrac{1}{3} mg = ma$, which gives $a = \dfrac{1}{3} g$.

Since the fireman must slide with at least this acceleration to keep the tension within the breaking limit, the minimum acceleration required is $\dfrac{1}{3} g$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3} g$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The resultant of two forces acting at an angle of $120^{{}^{\circ}}$ is $10 \mathrm{ kg}-\mathrm{W}$ and is perpendicular to one of the forces. That force is
questions.solution:
Let the two forces be $F_1$ and $F_2$. The angle between them is $\theta = 120^{{}^{\circ}}$. The resultant $R = 10 \text{ kg-W}$ is perpendicular to $F_1$.

The formula for the angle $\alpha$ that the resultant makes with $F_1$ is given by $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{F_2 \sin \theta}{F_1 + F_2 \cos \theta}$.

Since the resultant is perpendicular to $F_1$, $\alpha = 90^{{}^{\circ}}$, which implies $\tan 90^{{}^{\circ}} = \infty$. This occurs when the denominator is zero:

$F_1 + F_2 \cos 120^{{}^{\circ}} = 0$

$F_1 + F_2 (-0.5) = 0 \Rightarrow F_1 = 0.5 F_2 \Rightarrow F_2 = 2 F_1$.

The magnitude of the resultant $R$ is given by $R^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2 F_1 F_2 \cos 120^{{}^{\circ}}$.

Substituting $R = 10$ and $F_2 = 2 F_1$:

$10^2 = F_1^2 + (2 F_1)^2 + 2 F_1 (2 F_1) (-0.5)$

$100 = F_1^2 + 4 F_1^2 - 2 F_1^2$

$100 = 3 F_1^2$

$F_1^2 = \dfrac{100}{3} \Rightarrow F_1 = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ kg-W}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{3}} \mathrm{ kg}-\mathrm{W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The motion of a particle of mass $m$ is described by $y=u t+g t^{2}$. The force acting on the particle will be
questions.solution:
The displacement of the particle is given by $y = ut + gt^2$.

The velocity $v$ is the first derivative of displacement with respect to time $t$:

$v = \dfrac{dy}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(ut + gt^2) = u + 2gt$.

The acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity with respect to time $t$:

$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(u + 2gt) = 2g$.

The force $F$ acting on the particle is given by Newton's second law, $F = ma$:

$F = m(2g) = 2mg$.

Answer: $2 \mathrm{mg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
When a car of mass $m$ is moving with speed $v$ along a circle of radius $r$ on a level road, the centripetal force is provided by $f$, where $f$ denotes
$\left(\mu_{s} \rightarrow\right.$ coefficient of friction, $N \rightarrow$ normal reaction)
questions.solution:
For a car of mass $m$ moving in a circular path of radius $r$ with speed $v$ on a level road, the centripetal force required is given by $F_{c} = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$.

On a level road, this centripetal force is provided by the static frictional force $f$ acting between the tires and the road surface.

The static frictional force $f$ can take any value from $0$ up to the maximum limiting friction, which is given by $f_\max = \mu_{s}N$, where $\mu_{s}$ is the coefficient of static friction and $N$ is the normal reaction.

For the car to safely negotiate the turn without skidding, the required centripetal force must be less than or equal to the maximum available static friction. Thus, $f = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} \leq \mu_{s}N$.

Answer: $\dfrac{m v^{2}}{r}=f \leq \mu_{s} N$

questions.q: A body weight $50 \mathrm{ g}$ in air and $40 \mathrm{ g}$ in water. How much would it weight in a liquid of specific gravity $1.5$ ?
questions.solution:
Weight of body in air, m_{1}=50 g=5 $\times10^{-2} \mathrm{ kg}$ Weight of body in water, m_{2}=40 $\mathrm{ g}=4 \times10^{-2} \mathrm{ kg}$ Buoyant force on the body, $\begin{aligned} F^{\prime} &=m_{1} g-m_{2} g \\
&=g\left( m_{1}-m_{2}\right) \\
&=g\left(5 \times10^{-2}-4 \times10^{-2}\right) \\
F^{\prime} &=10^{-2} \mathrm{ g} \mathrm{ N}
\end{aligned}$ But buoyant force is given as $\begin{aligned} F^{\prime} &=V \rho g \\
10^{-2} \mathrm{ g}&=V \rho g \\
10^{-2} &=\rho \mathrm{V}\\
\Rightarrow \quad 10^{-2} &=10^{3} \mathrm{ V} \quad \text{ [From Eq. (i)] }\\
\Rightarrow \quad V &=10^{-5} \mathrm{ m}^{3} \quad\left[\because \rho=10^{3} \mathrm{ kg}/ \mathrmm^{3}\right] \\
\Rightarrow \quad \text{ Loss of weight in liquid }=\rho_{l} V g & {\left[\because \rho_{l}=1.5 \rho\right] } \\
W^{\prime} &=1.5 \rho \times10^{-5} \times10 \quad \\
=& 1.5 \times10^{3} \times10^{-5} \times10 \\
=& 0.15 \mathrm{ N}
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Loss of weight (in kg) $=\frac{w^{\prime}}{g}=\frac{0.15}{10}=0.015 \mathrm{ kg}=15 \mathrm{ g}\therefore$ Weight of body in water $=50-15=35 \mathrm{ g}$

questions.q: A uniform chain of length $L$ is lying partly on a table, the remaining part hanging down from the edge of the table. If the coefficient of friction between the chain and the table is $0.5$, what is the minimum length of the chain that should lie on the table, to prevent the chain from slipping down to the ground?
questions.solution:
Let length of chain lying the table be $y$.
Mass per unit length of the chain $=\frac{M}{L}$ Mass of the chain lying on the table, $M^{\prime}=\frac{M}{L} \cdot y$ Mass of the length $(L-y)$ of hanging chain $=\frac{M}{L}(L-y)$
At equilibrium,
Friction force between table and chain $=$ Weight of hanging part of the chain
$\mu\left(\frac{M}{L} y\right) g=\frac{M}{L}(L-y) g\Rightarrow \quad \mu y=L-y\Rightarrow \quad 0.5 y=L-y \quad[\because \mu=0.5]\Rightarrow \quad y=\frac{2 L}{3}$

questions.q: A body of mass $1 \mathrm{ kg}$ starting from origin with initial velocity of $3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}} \mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$. If a constant force of $2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathfrak{j}}$ acts on it, find the coordinate of point it reaches in $3 \mathrm{ s}$.
questions.solution:
Given, initial velocity, $u=3 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+4 \hat{\hat{\mathrm{s}}}$
Force, $F=2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$
Initial velocity along $X$-axis and $Y_{\text{-axis }}$ are $u_{x}=3 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ and $u_{y}=4 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$, respectively.
Similarly, $F_{x}=2 \mathrm{ N}$ and $F_{y}=-3 \mathrm{ N}$
If acceleration along $X and Y$-axes are $a_{x} and a_{y}$, then a_{x}=$\frac{F_{x}}{m}=\frac{2}{1}=2 \mathrm{ m}$/ $\mathrms^{2}$ \quad[\because F=m a] $\begin{aligned} a_{y} &=\frac{F_{y}}{m}=\frac{-3}{1}=-3 \mathrm{ m}/ \mathrms^{2} \\
s_{x} &=u_{x} t+\frac{1}{2} u_{x} l^{2}=3 \times3+\frac{1}{2} \times2 \times9=18 \mathrm{un}\\
s_{y} &=u_{y} t+\frac{1}{2} a_{y} t^{2}=4 \times3+\frac{1}{2} \times(-3) \times9 \\
&=12-13.5=-1.5 \mathrm{ m}
\end{aligned}$ So, required $x and y$-coordinates of point $=(18,-15)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A monkey of mass $40 \mathrm{ kg}$ climbs up a rope which can stand a maximum tension of $600 \mathrm{ N}$. The rope will break, when the monkey
options: climbs up with an acceleration $6 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$
climbs down with an acceleration of $4 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$
climbs up with uniform speed of $5 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$
slides down the rope freely under gravity
questions.solution:
Mass of the monkey, $m=40 \mathrm{~kg}$
Maximum tension that the rope can bear, $T_{\max }=600 \mathrm{~N}$
In option (a), acceleration of monkey, $a=6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrms^{2}$ (upward)
$\thereforeBy equation$ of motion,

\Rightarrow \quad$\begin{array}{ll}T & -m g=m a \\
T & =m(g+a) \\
& =40(10+6)=640 \mathrm{~N}
\end{array}$Since, $T \gt T_{\text{max }$}$, hence in this case, rope will break. Therefore, option (a) is correct.
In option (b), acceleration of monkey, $a=4 $\mathrm{~m}$ / \mathrms^{2}$ (downward)
$\thereforeBy equation$ of motion,

T=m(g-a)=40(10-4)=240 \mathrm{~N}Since,$T \lt  T_{\max }$, then the rope will not break.
In option (c), monkey climbs up with uniform speed, $v=5 $\mathrm{~m}$ / $\mathrm{s}\therefore$ Acceleration, $a=0 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrms^{2}$
Hence, by equation of motion, $T=m g$
=40 $\times$10=400 $\mathrm{~N}$Since, $T \lt  T_{\max }$, hence rope will not break.
In option $(\mathrm{d}$)$, acceleration, $a=g$
\therefore \quad T=m(g-a)=m(g-g)=0 \mathrm{~N} \text{. }Since, $T \lt  T_{\max }$, the rope will not break.
Therefore, only option (a) is correct.$
